clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive hereditary spastic paraplegia caused by biallelic mutations in AP5Z1, which encodes the zeta subunit of adaptor protein complex 5 (AP-5).
Onset is often in adult or later life; the phenotype may be pure or complicated with cognitive decline, neuropathy, parkinsonism, ataxia or sphincter disturbance.
AP-5 acts together with the SPG11 (spatacsin) and SPG15 (spastizin) proteins, so SPG48 shares a molecular pathway and phenotypic overlap with those thin-corpus-callosum disorders.
MRI may show a thin corpus callosum, white-matter change or subtle findings that overlap with the SPG11/SPG15 spectrum.

Because AP-5 governs late endosomal and lysosomal sorting and autophagic lysosome reformation, neurons accumulate storage-like material, giving SPG48 features of a mild lysosomal and autophagy disorder.
Onset is typically later than in SPG11 or SPG15, and some patients present chiefly with a slowly progressive spastic gait and bladder urgency.
Consider SPG48 in adult-onset complicated hereditary spastic paraplegia with a thin corpus callosum when SPG11 and SPG15 testing is negative.
reference.pathophysiology: AP5Z1 encodes the zeta subunit of adaptor protein complex 5 (AP-5), a heterotetrameric coat-like complex that, with its partners spatacsin (SPG11) and spastizin (SPG15), mediates protein sorting and cargo retrieval from late endosomes and lysosomes and supports autophagic lysosome reformation. Loss of functional AP-5 impairs endolysosomal traffic and autophagy, so undegraded material and abnormal storage bodies accumulate within neurons; the longest central motor axons of the corticospinal tracts are especially vulnerable to this failure of membrane trafficking and organelle recycling, producing a length-dependent axonopathy and progressive spasticity. Shared membership of the SPG11/SPG15/SPG48 pathway explains the common radiological signature of a thin corpus callosum and the overlapping complicated phenotype, while the storage-like pathology links this hereditary spastic paraplegia mechanistically to lysosomal disease.
additionalDifferentials: SPG11 (spatacsin) and SPG15 (spastizin) hereditary spastic paraplegia with thin corpus callosum
Other complicated recessive hereditary spastic paraplegias (SPG7, SPG54)
Lysosomal storage disorders with neurological involvement
Early-onset parkinsonism syndromes when parkinsonism is prominent
additionalInvestigations: AP5Z1 sequencing, usually within a hereditary spastic paraplegia or exome panel alongside SPG11 and SPG15
MRI brain and spine assessing corpus callosum thickness and white matter
Nerve conduction studies for associated neuropathy
Ophthalmological review, since retinal change can occur within this pathway group
Studies for storage material where a lysosomal mimic is suspected
redFlags: Rapid cognitive or motor decline suggesting an alternative neurodegenerative process
Prominent bulbar dysfunction with aspiration risk
A new sensory level or sphincter loss suggesting compressive myelopathy
Atypically rapid progression prompting reassessment of the diagnosis
reference.prognosis: Slowly progressive over years; ambulation is often maintained for a prolonged period in pure cases, whereas complicated disease with cognitive decline and neuropathy carries greater cumulative disability.
pitfalls: Stopping at SPG11 and SPG15 testing and missing AP5Z1 in the same molecular pathway
Overlooking the lysosomal and autophagy storage aspect and its diagnostic clues
Attributing adult-onset spasticity to multiple sclerosis without considering recessive hereditary spastic paraplegia
Assuming a normal corpus callosum excludes the diagnosis
